content: Psychological stress is a well-established factor that can exacerbate asthma symptoms. Written emotional disclosure, a therapeutic intervention where individuals write about traumatic or stressful experiences, has been shown to reduce stress and improve both physical and psychological health. This intervention may have potential benefits in managing asthma. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of written emotional disclosure for individuals with asthma. Specifically, the review aimed to assess: (1) whether emotional disclosure improves self-reported quality of life compared to writing about neutral topics, (2) whether it improves objective health outcomes, and (3) whether different types of emotional disclosure vary in their effectiveness for asthma management. To identify relevant studies, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Airways Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, AMED, and PsycINFO, with the most recent search completed in January 2014. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared written emotional disclosure with a control intervention involving emotionally neutral writing in individuals with asthma. Four studies, involving a total of 414 participants, met the inclusion criteria. Three studies focused on adults, while one included adolescents. The participants' ages ranged from 14 to 43 years, and the duration of the trials varied from two to twelve months. The interventions were based on Pennebaker's method of emotional disclosure. While the overall risk of bias in these studies was low, three of the four studies were at high risk of bias due to the lack of blinding of assessors, and one study was at high risk for selective reporting. The interpretation of the findings was further complicated by variations in outcome measures, measurement tools, control group methods, and follow-up schedules. When data from the four studies were pooled, the results showed an uncertain effect of written emotional disclosure on forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) % predicted at three months or less of follow-up (mean difference [MD] 3.43%, 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.61% to 7.47%; very low-quality evidence). Similarly, evidence from two studies indicated an uncertain effect on forced vital capacity (FVC) (standardized mean difference [SMD] -0.02, 95% CI -0.30 to 0.26; low-quality evidence) and asthma symptoms (SMD -0.22, 95% CI -0.52 to 0.09; low-quality evidence). However, there was some evidence suggesting that written emotional disclosure might improve asthma control at three months or less of follow-up (SMD 0.29, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.58; low-quality evidence). The data for other outcomes, such as quality of life, medication use, healthcare utilization, and psychological well-being, could not be pooled due to inconsistencies across studies. Individual trials did not demonstrate significant benefits of written emotional disclosure for these outcomes. However, one trial reported a significant reduction in beta-agonist use in the disclosure group compared to the control group at three months or less of follow-up (MD -1.62, 95% CI -2.62 to -0.62; low-quality evidence). The review did not address potential adverse effects of emotional writing. In conclusion, the evidence is insufficient to determine whether written emotional disclosure has a meaningful impact on asthma-related outcomes, including quality of life, psychological well-being, medication use, and healthcare utilization. The overall quality of the evidence was low, and better-designed studies with standardized outcome measures are needed to clarify the role of written emotional disclosure in asthma management.
